planting.note: Root dormant hardwood cuttings in late winter or plant bare-root vines in early spring against a sturdy fence, tree, or arbor in moist, fertile soil; winter grape climbs vigorously by tendrils along stream corridors and needs a strong support from the start.

directions: Plant against a fence, arbor, or large tree in moist, fertile bottomland soil in full sun to light shade; winter grape is a wide-ranging native liana of eastern floodplains and stream banks, historically confused with the closely related riverbank grape but distinguished by glossier, less deeply cut leaves and a smooth (not cobwebby) leaf underside. Its small, intensely fragrant spring flowers draw bees and other pollinating insects in large numbers, and the tart, blue-black grapes hang on the vine into late fall, sweetening after frost and feeding songbirds, foxes, and raccoons through the lean months. Because it climbs by tendril into the tree canopy rather than mounding as a shrub, give it a tall, sturdy support and prune hard each dormant season to keep growth manageable near structures.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root vines in late winter to early spring in consistently moist to wet soil in full sun to part shade against a fence, tree, or arbor; catbird grape naturally roots along riverbanks and swamp margins and tolerates periodic flooding far better than most cultivated grapes.

directions: Plant along a moist streambank, low woodland edge, or wet fence line in full sun to part shade; catbird grape is a striking native vine of the Mississippi Valley and Gulf South wetlands, named for its bright red young stems and deeply palmate, hand-shaped leaves that set it apart from every other native grape at a glance. It thrives in soggy, seasonally flooded ground where few other fruiting vines survive, making it a useful choice for rain gardens and low, wet corners of the landscape. The small, tart black grapes ripen in late summer and are quickly stripped by catbirds, thrashers, and other fruit-eating songbirds, while the inconspicuous spring flowers still provide an early nectar source for native bees. Give it a tall support and expect vigorous growth once the roots find consistent moisture.
sources: U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service — Species Profile

planting.note: Plant dormant hardwood cuttings or bare-root vines in late winter to early spring against a fence, shrub, or arbor in well-drained sandy soil in full sun to light shade; calloose grape is compact by grape standards and well suited to a smaller trellis or wildlife hedge in peninsular Florida and coastal south Alabama gardens.

directions: Plant in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to light shade against a fence or into the edge of a pineland or hammock planting; calloose grape is a compact, heat-tolerant native vine of central and south Florida pinelands and hammocks, easily told apart from the sprawling muscadine by its pointed leaves with dense, woolly, gray-white undersides and forked (rather than simple) tendrils. It stays smaller and more manageable than most wild grapes, reaching roughly 15 to 20 feet, which makes it a practical choice for a modest trellis or wildlife screen in a native Florida garden. The dark red to purple-black grapes ripen over summer and are eagerly taken by mockingbirds, cardinals, raccoons, and other wildlife, while the small spring flowers offer an early nectar source for native bees.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Plant nursery-grown divisions or container stock in spring at the margin of a pond, ditch, or bog garden in wet to consistently moist, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; coral greenbrier is an obligate wetland species and will struggle anywhere the soil dries out for extended periods.

directions: Plant at a pond margin, in a bog garden, or along a wooded stream edge in consistently wet to moist, acidic soil in partial shade to full sun; coral greenbrier is a deciduous, tendril-climbing native vine of southeastern swamp forests and pocosins, easily identified among its evergreen relatives by its thinner, less prickly stems and its dropped leaves in winter. It is one of the few native greenbriers that stands out visually in a naturalistic planting, producing showy clusters of bright coral-red berries in fall that persist into winter and are an important food source for waterfowl, songbirds, and other wetland wildlife. Because it depends on saturated or seasonally flooded soil to thrive, it is best used in rain gardens, retention pond edges, or other low spots rather than average garden beds.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service — Species Profile

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in spring in well-drained, sandy soil in full sun to light shade; dune greenbrier is adapted to exposed coastal dunes and maritime scrub and tolerates salt spray, wind, and drought once its deep rhizome system is established.

directions: Plant in well-drained sandy soil in full sun to light shade on a dune, coastal fence line, or sandy woodland edge; dune greenbrier is an evergreen, salt-tolerant native vine of Gulf and Atlantic coastal dunes and maritime scrub, recognizable by its rounded, fiddle- or heart-shaped leaves that lack the marginal spines found on many other greenbriers. Its dense evergreen cover and stabilizing rhizome network make it valuable for holding sandy soil on exposed coastal sites where few other flowering vines persist. Small clusters of inconspicuous spring flowers give way to dark berries relished by mockingbirds, towhees, and other coastal wildlife, and the tangled growth offers year-round cover for ground-nesting birds. Once established it needs no supplemental irrigation and handles the salt spray and drought of an unshaded dune planting without difficulty.
sources: Atlas of Florida Plants (University of South Florida)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions or container stock in spring in moist, humus-rich to sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; false chinaroot dies back to its tuberous rhizome each winter and re-sprouts thornless new growth the following spring, so mark its location to avoid disturbing the dormant crown.

directions: Plant at a woodland edge, damp thicket, or bog garden margin in moist, humus-rich to sandy soil in partial shade to full sun; false chinaroot is an unusually well-mannered native greenbrier of the Atlantic coastal plain, dying back to a starchy underground rhizome each fall and sending up thornless, tendril-climbing stems each spring rather than persisting as a tangled evergreen thicket. Its modest, well-behaved size makes it one of the few Smilax species suited to a smaller garden bed rather than a wild naturalized area. Inconspicuous spring flowers provide early-season forage for native bees, and the blue-black berries that follow feed thrushes, catbirds, and other woodland birds through fall. The starchy rhizomes were historically processed by Indigenous peoples into a food starch, giving the plant its common name in reference to the true chinaroot (Smilax china) of Asia.
sources: North Carolina State University Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service — Species Profile
